title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] Introducing Haiku DPO: a synthetically generated Direct Preference Optimization dataset. It consists of user prompts for a haiku and generations scored for "correctness".
You can directly use this dataset for DPO, but it may also be interesting for exploring other questions 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GD54jfxboAAkEsH.jpg
────────
[2/10] Synthetic data and DPO are big topics in AI. I wanted to learn more about them at the start of the year. The two biggest lessons I took from @fastdotai and @jeremyphoward are:
📚 I learn best by doing
💡 You can contribute to ML without massive resources by being creative.
────────
[3/10] Preference datasets usually rely on human annotators or GPT-4. Asking friends and family to help label data won't make me popular. GPT-4 is expensive and has become a sledgehammer used for all tasks. Are there alternative ways to rank preference?
────────
[4/10] A haiku is a poem that *usually* follows a 5-7-5 syllable structure. This means scoring generated haiku via some fairly simple Python code is possible. This removes one of the most significant expenses for preference datasets: ranking results.
────────
[5/10] Large proprietary models are often used for generating synthetic datasets. While this may be the best approach for certain tasks, I found that @teknium's OpenHermes-2.5-Mistral-7B model already performs well, with some room for improvement.
────────
[6/10] 🤔 Because we are able to rank results cheaply, we can also potentially now begin to explore questions like:
📏 how far apart in quality do "accepted" and "rejected" responses need to be?
🔀 should we remove ties?
📊 is more data better, or is it better to focus on quality?
────────
[7/10] I used @argilla_io's excellent Distilabel to construct this dataset using a few hours of @GoogleColab time.
────────
[8/10] A 7B model is small enough that it's possible to assess the impact of different approaches to constructing a DPO dataset fairly quickly, and because we can easily score the generations, we can quickly iterate.
────────
[9/10] The notebooks for creating this dataset are messy, but I've begun sharing them here:
I think creating synthetic datasets can be a key way for the community to contribute to open AI, so I'll write this up as a tutorial to try and help others get started.
────────
[10/10] This is a WIP, but you can access the datasets on the @huggingface Hub.
Next steps:
- Train some models on this data: initially 7B, but I want to explore how far I can get making a ~1B model at writing haiku

paper page:
The Internet's wealth of content, with up to 60% published in English, starkly contrasts the global population, where only 18.8% are English speakers, and just 5.1% consider it their native language, leading to disparities in online information access. Unfortunately, automated processes for dubbing of video - replacing the audio track of a video with a translated alternative - remains a complex and challenging task due to pipelines, necessitating precise timing, facial movement synchronization, and prosody matching. While end-to-end dubbing offers a solution, data scarcity continues to impede the progress of both end-to-end and pipeline-based methods. In this work, we introduce Anim-400K, a comprehensive dataset of over 425K aligned animated video segments in Japanese and English supporting various video-related tasks, including automated dubbing, simultaneous translation, guided video summarization, and genre/theme/style classification.

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel) — thread (6 tweets)
summary:
[1/6] Which are the most impactful synthetic datasets on the @huggingface Hub? First, find these datasets using the new `synthetic` tag.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GF5cEAZaEAAN4e-.jpg
────────
[2/6] ❤️ let us start by looking at the most liked datasets in this category.
Unsurprisingly, @teknium's OpenHermes-2.5 leads, with the WebSight dataset and @argilla_io's datasets not far behind.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GF5cEjja0AAjXo3.png
────────
[3/6] ⏬ @argilla_io's distilabel-intel-orca-dpo-pairs dataset has had an enormous impact. It's a cleaned and improved dataset created using Distilabel. Contributing to open ML through data curation and improvement can be very impactful.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GF5cFHmbEAATN76.png
────────
[4/6] Download counts alone don't show the full impact. We can also look at the number of models trained with these datasets. Note that the count may be underestimated if data isn't specifiedW. Contribute by including metadata for your training dataset.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GF5cFq8aAAAlKnY.png
────────
[5/6] Are you skeptical about the number of models trained on a dataset? Don't worry, we can look at the total number of downloads for all models trained on that dataset. These datasets enable popular and used models!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GF5cGL0aoAA8tGQ.png
────────
[6/6] This analysis isn't perfect because the data isn't perfect. You can improve this by:
🔧 Adding a `synthetic` tag to your dataset if it's synthetic
🔧 Adding the dataset used to train your models

[1/2] Many (open) LLMs struggle with complex reasoning. UltraInteract from @OpenBMB is a comprehensive alignment dataset created for intricate reasoning tasks which might be able to help address this gap.

🔗 diverse reasoning chains with various planning strategies presented in a unified format
🔄 multi-turn interaction trajectories involving both the environment and the critique
👥 pairwise data to aid preference learning
The dataset includes 86k instructions, 286k correct answers, and 219k pairs and has an MIT licence.

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel)
summary:
🔍 CodeEditorBench: Evaluating LLMs on Code Editing Tasks
The CodeEditorBench dataset, from @GeZhang86038849 et al., aims to assess the code editing capabilities of large language models (LLMs) across four scenarios:
1. Code debugging 🐞
2. Code translation 🌐
3. Code polishing ✨
4. Code requirement switching 🔄
The dataset curates diverse coding challenges from five sources, spanning various programming languages and complexity levels rather than focusing solely on code generation.
📊 LLM Evaluation Results:
• 19 LLMs were evaluated on CodeEditorBench
• Closed-source models, particularly Gemini-Ultra and GPT-4, outperformed open-source models across all tasks
🌟 Dataset Stats:
• 1,200+ coding challenges
• 5 diverse data sources
• Multiple programming languages
• Varying complexity levels
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GKojbiFWAAAP2U4.jpg

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel)
summary:
Domain-specific evals are crucial for understanding LLMs' real-world capabilities. We need more!
Inspired by discussions at a recent @CILIPinfo conference on how librarians use AI, I compared GPT-4, Claude, and Mistral in helping generate advanced PubMed search queries.
Results showed:
🔍 Wide variation in search result counts (0 to 400K+)
🤔 Some models struggled to use valid MeSH terms
❌ A few models generated queries that failed in the PubMed API
I've open-sourced the code and data on GitHub. This required coding, but I hope we'll build tools to make building evals more widely accessible.
Looking forward to discussing how librarians can do this kind of evaluation of AI at @cilipireland conference 🤗
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GKviAWEXIAAV8lb.jpg

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel)
summary:
Could DPO-style preference data be crucial for enhancing open LLMs across different languages?
Leveraging a 7k preference dataset, @argilla_io, @huggingface, and @kaist_ai utilized @kaist_ai's ORPO technique with the latest @MistralAI MOE model to create a very high-performing open LLM.
Since ORPO doesn't require a separate SFT stage, all that is needed is a strong base model + high-quality DPO-style datasets.
Currently, there is a major lack of non-English DPO datasets. Could filling this gap significantly improve open LLMs in various languages?
This Space provides an overview of the current state of DPO datasets across different languages:

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] Only 14 languages have DPO preference style datasets on the @huggingface Hub. Let's improve that! How?
The @CohereForAI Aya dataset has human-annotated prompt-completion pairs in 71 languages. We can use this to create DPO datasets for more languages!
────────
[2/5] Using Aya's prompt/response pairs as a starting point we can use an LLM to generate an additional response to each prompt. We then use an LLM Judge to rank each response. If you don't know the Aya dataset yet find it here:
────────
[3/5] In some/many languages, human responses may be better than LLM ones. We use @argilla_io's distilabel library to push data to Argilla for validation. This helps determine if an LLM judge is effective for different languages.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/1786390323557728256/pu/img/IvEdlCC3XV2zUFjH.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1786390323557728256/pu/vid/avc1/334x270/Dy0ZJu8rp-dEPJnP.mp4?tag=12
────────
[4/5] As an example of what this pipeline produces:
- a DPO style dataset for Dutch using Llama 3 as a generator/judge LM.
- An annotation Space that anyone with a HF account can contribute to:
────────
[5/5] As part of Data is Better Together we want to build more DPO datasets. Join us here!

[2/4] ColPali has faced criticism for being impractical due to limited multivector support in many vector DBs. However, two DBs that do support multivectors are:
- @vespaengine:
- @qdrant_engine:
────────
[3/4] I would also highly recommend checking out @bclavie's library: an excellent way to use ColPali with minimal code. If you have a bunch of PDFs you want to retrieve, I'd highly recommend starting here.

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel) — thread (6 tweets)
summary:
[1/6] How do you release an impactful dataset on the @huggingface Hub?
We're enhancing how we track dataset downloads on the Hub, so I wanted to share some common themes I've noticed for datasets with high downloads. 🧵
────────
[2/6] 1️⃣ Curated and refined datasets
@argilla_io shows how to enhance datasets (like those from @databricks) with extra curation and cleaning—an underexplored way to support open-source AI.
Over 200,000 monthly downloads.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GagUK53bMAA2YXD.jpg
────────
[3/6] @maximelabonne's open-perfectblend is another example in this genre. It was only released recently, but I wouldn't be surprised to see it get 1K+ downloads in the first month.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GagUMD6aQAAyNUU.jpg
────────
[4/6] 2️⃣ Synthetic data
Synthetic data lets the community create massive datasets. One developer can release 1M+ rows to train cutting-edge models. @teknium's OpenHermes-2.5 is getting over 2,000 downloads per month
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GagUNJ8bEAEYROD.jpg
────────
[5/6] Beyond raw downloads, this dataset has been used to train many models:
If you want to track when a new model is trained on a dataset, use this tool: to set up tracking.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GagUOKKaUAAu2tp.jpg
────────
[6/6] If you are a company building models and datasets, we've also just shipped new repository analytics so you can see how the community is using your models and downloads. You can get access to that via Enterprise Hub 🤗
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GagUQRxbMAAoUnZ.jpg

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] Is your desktop full of random screenshots? I just wrote a blog post on using @MistralAI's Pixtral (via @LMStudioAI) to automatically organize screenshots—no cloud APIs needed, so you can keep the weird memes you collect private!
Post here: More info 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GardAbfbAAA3yqK.jpg
────────
[2/7] @LMStudioAI recently added support for Pixtral (based on incredible work from @Prince_Canuma's MLX-VLM). They also added a headless mode for their OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
They already had structured generation (via @dottxtai Outlines). Enough to help me sort my screenshots?
────────
[3/7] I use the VLM to describe my screenshot using a structured output schema.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GardCaWaAAAdYLg.jpg
────────
[4/7] The structured output makes it possible to work directly with the VLM's outputs without a bunch of praying and string parsing. Slap a for loop on this, and my desktop will be less of a mess.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GardDahaAAItIyC.jpg
────────
[5/7] Running on my Mac M1, each image takes ~60 to process. For running in the background, this doesn't seem too bad.
────────
[6/7] While running stuff locally can be slower than cloud APIs, you get:
• Privacy (data stays on your machine)
• No API costs
• Full control over the pipeline—no rate limits
────────
[7/7] I'm excited to see more VLMs available on local devices. I'm particularly keen to see if anyone can get @rhymes_ai_'s Aria running locally (looking at you, @Prince_Canuma!).

Significant that the dataset used to create this is open. Open model developers are becoming increasingly transparent about their training approaches, but IMO if labs share training datasets, open-source model developers will have a massive advantage over closed-source.
Quoting @madiator
Introducing Bespoke-Stratos-32B, our reasoning model distilled from DeepSeek-R1 using Berkeley NovaSky’s Sky-T1 recipe.
The model outperforms Sky-T1 and o1-preview in reasoning (Math and Code) benchmarks and almost reaches the performance of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B while being trained on 47x fewer examples!
Crucially, we open-source the dataset (DeepSeek open-sourced the model, not the data). Let's work together on this exciting direction of reasoning distillation!
🧵More info and link to the blog below!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gh6kX1xaUAEJsE8.png

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Can @googlegemma DiffusionGemma help fix broken OCR?
In theory, denoising tokens in parallel could work better for OCR correction since context is seen upfront?
Pointed it at 19th-century newspaper OCR. It corrected better than the autoregressive baseline — at ~8x the speed.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2064931470251048960/img/kdS0_AmqaNUB39gt.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/2064931470251048960/vid/avc1/320x360/6Prg9GeaBR0E-haG.mp4?tag=27
────────
[2/8] Results:
- CER 0.066 → 0.036 (DiffusionGemma) vs 0.042 (Gemma-4)
- fixed 85% of OCR errors vs 62%
- median 1.7s vs 14.7s per passage
- ~10 denoising steps vs ~200 sequential tokens
────────
[3/8] The setup: 75 passages of BLN600 (19th-century British Library newspapers with human ground-truth transcriptions), DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B vs Gemma-4-E4B, identical prompt, bf16, one A100.
────────
[4/8] One idea went the wrong way: I expected the diffusion model to over-correct less ("it just denoises"). But it did the opposite; it edits more aggressively in both directions. Greedy AR decoding is the conservative editor (0.4% vs 1.4% of already-correct text touched).
────────
[5/8] A day-one experimental model beating its AR cousin on quality and speed on this task. I guess fine-tuning could make this a lot better?
────────
[6/8] In the transformers source: generate() accepts an undocumented starting canvas (decoder_input_ids). So I seeded it with the OCR text itself, i.e. "here's a nearly-right draft, denoise it."
────────
[7/8] Try it: live demo on @huggingface ZeroGPU with the step-by-step denoising replay, side-by-side diffs vs the human transcription, and the full benchmark table.
────────
[8/8] For me, this was a negative result: 2–5 steps, but it barely edits with 61/75 outputs identical to the noisy input. Real text is off-distribution as noise, so the sampler just accepts it maybe? (You can try this in the demo)

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Yesterday: diffusion LM beats AR on OCR correction.
Today, after a suggestion from the @GoogleDeepMind team: bench it against its parameter-matched twin instead (same 26B MoE, same 4B active).
The twin wins slightly on quality. The diffusion model is still ~10× faster.
Updated scoreboard
CER on 19th-c newspaper OCR (lower = better):
• OCR input: 0.066
• Gemma-4-E4B: 0.042 (15.3s/passage)
• DiffusionGemma: 0.035 (1.7s 🚀)
• Gemma-4-26B MoE: 0.027 (16.3s)
Equal capacity: diffusion trades accuracy for an order of magnitude of speed.
Also tried the suggested sampler fixes (thx @joao_gante!) for the "seeded canvas just copies its input" bug. They free the model from copying but it re-derives the input instead of correcting it. Might still be some tweaking here?

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] I ran 10 newer OCR models on @allen_ai's olmOCR-bench "old scans" subset.
The ranking flips depending on what you actually want. On the headline score, PaddleOCR-VL beats NuExtract3 (38.6 vs 37.8). But rank by how much of the page each model actually reads, and NuExtract3 is well ahead (41.6 vs 31.2). Same two models, opposite order.
The score rewards dropping boilerplate, i.e. letterheads, stamps, page numbers, so a model that reads the page more faithfully can rank lower.
IMO this is because a lot of VLM-based OCR models were made to provide tokens for training. It's less useful if you want faithful OCR of the whole page, like an archive where the letterhead is part of the record.
Two other things: a 1B model (LightOnOCR-2) has the best raw transcription in the field, and PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 sometimes hallucinates Chinese characters on English scans.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMo3uHjX0AAmwuT.jpg
────────
[2/2] Write-up + plus how I ran the whole thing on HF Jobs, no local GPU:

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel)
summary:

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel)
summary:
Your coding agent can now do semantic search to find models and datasets on the @huggingface Hub!
means you can hand it a prompt like:
"Find recent datasets of video game gameplay useful for training game-playing agents. Curate the best ones into a collection with a brief description for each."
...and it goes and does it.
I built hf find (a hf extension) to give agents a way to look up what's actually on the Hub: semantic search over 1.17M model and dataset cards, ranked by meaning.
It detects when an agent is driving and switches to TSV with hints on stderr (--format json for scripts), and every result ends with the next command to run, so it can go from search to find-similar to the card on its own. The index refreshes daily from a scheduled HF Job for about 5 cents a day.
Still some rough edges but quite cool to see agents use tools like this!
hf extensions install davanstrien/hf-find

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel)
summary:
Making Meta's "Recycling the Web" dataset likely cost ~$369k in 2025. Today the same data would cost ~$28k. I checked for $11!
The data recipe rewrites discarded low-quality web pages from @CommonCrawl into pre-training data with an LLM. I got an agent to re-implement it with datatrove on @huggingface Jobs.
In 2026, a 9B model beats the paper's own 70B teacher:
→ Qwen3.5-9B clears the quality gate 61.7% of the time vs the 70B's 49.6%
→ blind paired judges prefer the 9B's rewrites 20-4
What it cost:
→ whole PoC: ~$11 in GPU time, 4 models compared
→ the 9B arm: $0.60 for 600 docs - about $0.64 per million kept tokens
→ at that rate, Meta's released 44.4B-token set would be ≈ $28k to reproduce. At the 70B teacher's rate ($8.30/M): ≈ $369k (Naive linear extrapolation.)
The original: filter never released, only part of the data shipped.
This version: everything's open, including the pipeline, all 1,953 rewrites, cost receipts, and a 30s CPU script that re-scores every rewrite. If you don't trust my agent's eval, run the check yourself!
Feel free to run this at scale: REPRODUCE.md in the repo walks the whole pipeline, and scaling up is two numbers in the executor. If you rebuild the full 44.4B-token set, I'd love to see it!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNwd3QOXcAAjJEA.jpg

title: Daniel van Strien (@vanstriendaniel)
summary:
Training an object detector is easy when you already have labelled boxes. If you're working on a new domain or task, you often don't.
I've been experimenting with using an agent to bootstrap the data instead:
– a zero-shot model labels a sample (@TIIuae Falcon-Perception, 0.6B, Apache-2.0)
– a small student learns from it (~30M params, one small GPU)
– the student goes back over the pages the teacher called "empty", a VLM judge checks its finds, retrain
– rinse and repeat one or two times
I think agents plus smallish specialist models like Falcon-Perception can make building domain-specific object detectors, image classifiers, etc. much easier. The small models are still very valuable once you work at scale (used this to cut 411,385 illustrations out of 115k Britannica pages for about $2 of inference).
Wrapped this up as a skill so you can try it: point your agent at a bucket of images and one class name ("illustration", "stamp", "table") and it runs the whole thing on @huggingface Jobs. You check the labels a few times along the way.
try it here:

────────
[2/2] The real tokenmaxxing move: use frontier agents to build small classifiers for large-scale data curation.
Small classifiers already help curate the data used to train LLMs. I wanted to see how far an agent could take me in building one.
I used Astra, SetFit and @huggingface Jobs to turn 200 agent-labelled examples into a reusable document-purpose classifier, reviewing the categories and tricky cases along the way.
It classified 191,724 FinePDFs-Edu documents for ~$0.70 in inference compute, versus an estimated $13–26 to label the same document excerpts with low-cost batch LLMs.
Training experiments added ~$2.90 in compute.

clean_title: Declaring runtime requirements in UV scripts with huggingface_hub 1.32
summary:
UV scripts are a nice single-file way to share something runnable: dependencies live in the header; uv does the rest.
Often a script also needs a specific runtime, i.e. a specific vLLM image. This then usually lived in a README next to the script.
New in huggingface_hub 1.32: the script can declare that too, in a [tool.hf-jobs] table in the same header. A plain hf jobs uv run then does the right thing on @huggingface Jobs.
Docs:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSahsRPWwAAjh-0.jpg
clean_summary:
UV scripts let you share runnable code in a single file, with dependencies listed in the header and UV handling the rest. Usually, if a script needs a specific runtime, like a particular vLLM image, that info lived separately in a README.

Daniel van Strien explains that huggingface_hub 1.32 adds a way to declare the runtime directly in the script header using a [tool.hf-jobs] table. This means running hf jobs uv run automatically picks the right runtime on Hugging Face Jobs, simplifying how you share and run scripts.

summary:
Trained a Jev-style classifier on @huggingface Jobs for ~$1.50.
It's a 194M GLiNER2 model that suggests task tags for any Hub dataset from its column names and first row, and returns a label with a probability.
Zero-shot, GLiNER2's first suggestion matched an owner's tag 10% of the time. After 17 minutes of fine-tuning: 69%. The fine-tuned model runs on a free CPU in about a second.
Owners' tags are noisy, so some "wrong" answers are tags the owner left out.
The recipe is open: one hf jobs command trains the same kind of model on your own labels. The README example (book titles) runs in ~2 minutes for about $0.02.

Quoting @vanstriendaniel

It's a 194M GLiNER2 model that suggests task tags for any Hub dataset from its column names and first row, and returns a label with a probability.
Zero-shot, GLiNER2's first suggestion matched an owner's tag 10% of the time. After 17 minutes of fine-tuning: 69%. The fine-tuned model runs on a free CPU in about a second.
Owners' tags are noisy, so some "wrong" answers are tags the owner left out.
